answers.question: How does the O3 frontend format a date for display according to the user's locale, including showing "Today" for the current day? Point to the documentation and implementation.

paragraphs.text: The O3 frontend formats dates through one utility, `formatDate`, which lives in the framework package `@openmrs/esm-framework` (a shared library of UI/utility code that all O3 apps import). It is locale-aware because it delegates the actual formatting to the browser's built-in `Intl` API rather than hard-coding patterns, and it special-cases "today" by producing the word for today in the active language.

| Piece | Location |
|---|---|
| Implementation | `packages/framework/esm-utils/src/dates/date-util.ts` in `github.com/openmrs/openmrs-esm-core` |
| Generated API doc | `packages/framework/esm-framework/docs/functions/formatDate.md` |
| Developer guide | `content/en-US/docs/recipes/format-dates.mdx` in `github.com/openmrs/openmrs-contrib-o3-docs` |
The developer-facing documentation is the recipe "Formatting dates", which describes the same defaults and behaviour as the code [1]. There is a French translation of it at [2].
## Step by step: how a date becomes a display string

1. **The app calls `formatDate(date, options)`** [3]. The options are merged over `defaultOptions`, which is `{ mode: 'standard', time: 'for today', day: true, month: true, year: true, noToday: false }` [4].

2. **The locale is resolved** with `getLocale()` unless the caller passed one. `getLocale()` reads `window.i18next.language` — the language i18next picked from the `lang` attribute, a `?lang=` URL parameter, localStorage or the browser — normalizes it to a BCP 47 tag (the standard "language-REGION" form, e.g. `en-GB`), and patches the Haitian Creole tag `ht` to `fr-HT` [5]. The result is wrapped in an `Intl.Locale` for structured access [6].

3. **The calendar is chosen.** `getDefaultCalendar` returns the calendar registered for the locale, or falls back to the browser's resolved default calendar for that locale [7]. Registrations live in the `LocaleCalendars` class, which looks up a language-region key first, then the bare language, and caches the browser default [8]. Calendars can be registered with `registerDefaultCalendar(locale, calendar)` [9]; the O3 shell does this from the styleguide's `preferredCalendar` config [10].

4. **"Today" handling.** The date is tested with dayjs's `isToday` plugin [11]. If it is today and `noToday` is not set, the word for "today" is produced by `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` with `numeric: 'auto'`, which yields the localized word (e.g. "Today", "Heute") rather than a relative phrase, and the first letter is upper-cased in a locale-correct way [12]. `noToday` also defaults to `true` for Amharic (`am`), where localized "today" handling is skipped [13].

5. **Ordinary dates are formatted** by building `Intl.DateTimeFormatOptions` from the `year`/`month`/`day`/`numberingSystem` options and formatting into parts with `Intl.DateTimeFormat.formatToParts` [14]. For English, the locale is swapped to `en-GB` so that times show as AM/PM but the day-month order stays non-American [15].

6. **Separators and cleanup.** For English and Amharic in `standard` mode with both year and day present, the spaces between parts are replaced with hyphens (giving `16-May-2023`); in `wide` mode the separator becomes an em dash with spaces (`16 — May — 2023`) [16]. The `formatParts` helper does that replacement while leaving the separator before an era alone [17]. For the Ethiopic calendar the era marker and its preceding separator are stripped [18]. Parts are then joined into the final string [19].

7. **Time is appended** with a comma and a space when `time` is `true`, or when the date is today and `time` is `'for today'` — which is why "Today, 08:21" appears by default [20]. The time itself comes from `formatTime`, which uses `toLocaleTimeString` with 2-digit hour and minute, so 12- or 24-hour display follows the locale [21].
The full option shape is documented in the `FormatDateOptions` type, including the `noToday` flag and the `time: true | false | 'for today'` tri-state [22].

```mermaid
---
title: formatDate decision flow
---
flowchart TD
  call["formatDate(date, options)"] --> locale["Resolve locale via getLocale"]
  locale --> calendar["Resolve calendar via getDefaultCalendar"]
  calendar --> today{"Is the date today and not noToday?"}
  today -->|yes| word["Intl.RelativeTimeFormat numeric auto gives the localized word for Today"]
  today -->|no| fmt["Intl.DateTimeFormat formatToParts"]
  fmt --> sep["Replace separators for en and am, or use em dash in wide mode"]
  sep --> join["Join parts into a string"]
  word --> timeq{"Include time?"}
  join --> timeq
  timeq -->|"time true or today with for today"| append["Append comma and formatTime output"]
  timeq -->|no| done["Return the string"]
  append --> done
```
## Related helpers in the same file

`formatDatetime` simply calls `formatDate` with `time: true` [23]. `formatPartialDate` handles values that may only have a year or year-month (common for approximate clinical dates): it parses the string with `any-date-parser` using the current locale, turns off the option for any part that was missing, and delegates to `formatDate` [24]. `isOmrsDateToday` exposes the same dayjs `isToday` check on its own [25].

I read the English docs recipe and its French counterpart, the generated `formatDate` API page, `get-locale.ts` and `date-util.ts`; I did not trace every O3 app that consumes these utilities, and I did not read the shell code that maps the styleguide `preferredCalendar` setting onto `registerDefaultCalendar`, so the exact wiring of that config is described from the docs only [26].

code: OpenMRS provides several utilities to work with dates. These utilities have been designed with locale sensitivity in mind. Acceptable date formats vary by language and region, and the functions are intended to accommodate that variation.
## Utilities for formatting dates for display
This utility accepts a `Date` object and returns a string. It formats the input date according to the current locale and the given parameters:
The mode parameter can be set to `standard` or `wide`.

For English dates, `standard` mode displays a date such as `16-May-2023`, while `wide` mode displays a date such as `16 — May — 2023`. Other locales may use locale-specific month names, calendars, and punctuation.

By default, `formatDate` uses `{ mode: "standard", time: "for today", day: true, month: true, year: true, noToday: false }`. If the date is today, then `Today` is produced instead of the actual day in the locale language, and the time is appended because the default `time` option is `"for today"`. Pass `{ time: false }` to suppress the time for today's date, or `{ noToday: true }` to format today like any other date.

When the `time` option is set to `true`, the time is appended with a comma and a space, e.g. `16-May-2023, 08:21`. This format agrees with the output of `Date.prototype.toLocaleString` for most locales.
